subject: Art & Design
title: Greek Columns: The Three Classical Orders
description: One-minute skill: Greek Columns: The Three Classical Orders.

hook.text: Walk past any courthouse, bank, or parliament and you'll see Greek columns. A 2,500-year-old design, still used.

buildup.text: The three Greek orders: Doric (simple), Ionic (scrolled), and Corinthian (ornate leaves). Each has a distinct look.

discovery.text: Doric says strength. Ionic says knowledge. Corinthian says wealth. Architects chose based on a building's purpose.

twist.text: The Parthenon's columns aren't straight. They bulge slightly in the middle to correct an optical illusion.

climax.text: Romans added Tuscan and Composite orders. But the original three remain architecture's most recognized forms.

punchline.text: Three column styles. Thousands of years. Still the language of authority.

quiz.question: What are the three Greek column orders from simplest to most ornate?

details.summary: Greek architecture developed three column orders — Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian — each with distinct proportions and decorative details. Doric is sturdy and plain, Ionic is slender with scroll capitals, and Corinthian is ornate with acanthus leaf carvings.
details.whyItMatters: The three orders gave architects a shared language of proportion and decoration that persists today. Government buildings, banks, and museums worldwide still use Greek columns to signal authority and permanence.
takeaways: Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian define the three Greek orders
Each has distinct proportions and capital decorations
These orders remain the vocabulary of Western architecture

faq.question: What is the difference between the three orders?
faq.answer: Doric columns are thick with no base and simple slab capitals. Ionic columns are thinner with scroll-shaped (volute) capitals. Corinthian columns are the most slender and ornate, topped with carved acanthus leaves. Each order has matching rules for the entablature above.

faq.question: Why do so many modern buildings use Greek columns?
faq.answer: Greek columns symbolize democracy, learning, and authority. When Western nations built government and civic buildings, they deliberately copied Greek forms to link themselves to Athenian democratic ideals. The association is now deeply embedded in architectural culture.
